passage:
Week one: Over roasted corn by the lake in Bhopal, Shreya asked Ritu whether they might move in together after graduation. Ritu laughed it off and talked about a solo trek she was planning.
Week two: Shreya raised it again, her voice gentle. Ritu said, "I just like my space," picked up her bag and left early. That night, alone in her room, she scrolled for hours and felt a hollowness she couldn't name.
Week four: Ritu sent a message before she could stop herself: "I think I run because needing you scares me. I don't know how to do this, but I don't want to leave." Shreya replied, "Then let's go slow. Tea on Sunday?"

qa.q: What did Ritu talk about when Shreya first raised moving in?
qa.a: She talked about a solo trek she was planning.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling alone in her room that night, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt lonely and empty; she scrolled for hours and felt a hollowness she couldn't name.

qa.q: What was the turning point in week four?
qa.a: Ritu admitted in a message that needing Shreya scared her and that she didn't want to leave, which opened a slower way forward.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt when Ritu left early in week two?
qa.a: She may have felt rejected and unsure, having raised the topic gently.

grounding: A young woman guards her freedom and leaves when her partner asks for more, then admits the loneliness and fear of needing someone underneath.

passage: Kunal, you're asking old Wasim bhai why I never pushed you to talk at lunch? Because at twenty I was a lot like you. There was a girl I cared about, Firdaus. Every time she said, "Tell me what's on your mind," I'd crack a joke and change the subject. When she asked if I would meet her parents, I stopped calling. Told myself I was a free bird. The truth? I'd lie awake in my hostel room feeling like the loneliest man in Aligarh. I was scared that if I needed her and she left, I'd fall apart. I said that sentence out loud for the first time at thirty-two. Anyway. Your chai's getting cold.

qa.q: What did Wasim do when Firdaus asked about meeting her parents?
qa.a: He stopped calling.

qa.q: What was Wasim afraid of behind all his distance?
qa.a: He was scared that if he needed Firdaus and she left, he would fall apart.

qa.q: What choice did young Wasim make each time Firdaus asked for more, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He joked, changed the subject or stopped calling, which kept his freedom but left him lying awake lonely.

qa.q: How might Firdaus have experienced Wasim's jokes and silence?
qa.a: She likely felt shut out and confused, as if her questions were unwelcome.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls avoiding deep talks and leaving when a partner asked for more, with loneliness and fear of dependence underneath.

passage: When Mehak asked if I'd come to her sister's wedding in Jaipur and meet everyone, I heard myself say, "Let's not get heavy." Two weeks later I ended it, by text, from the library. I told my roommate I needed my freedom, that I'd never been one for all that. I'm Sabina, twenty-one, and here's what I didn't say: that night I ate dinner alone in the hostel mess and felt like the loneliest person in the building. I think I left because being needed felt like a trap, and needing her felt worse, like standing at the edge of something with no railing. I'm not ready to fix it. I'm starting to see it, at least.

qa.q: Where was Mehak's sister's wedding?
qa.a: In Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling underneath the talk of freedom?
qa.a: Sabina felt deeply lonely and afraid of depending on Mehak, not a lack of feeling.

qa.q: What could Sabina try next, now that the pattern is clearer?
qa.a: Talk it through with a trusted friend or counsellor, and practise saying small true things before walking away.

qa.q: How might Mehak have experienced a break-up by text after the wedding invitation?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt shocked and hurt, having asked for more closeness and been left instead.

grounding: Shows a young adult who avoids deep talk and leaves when a partner asks for more, while feeling lonely and afraid of dependence.

passage:
Warden's note, Room 214. Disha, second year, is fiercely independent: fixes her own fan, never asks for anything, eats early to avoid the crowd. Tonight her boyfriend waited at the gate for an hour. The guard said he wanted to "talk about where this is going". Disha sent word she was busy, then sat in the common room with a book she never turned a page of. When I asked if she was all right, she said, "I just don't do the needy stuff." Later I heard her on the phone to her mother, voice thick, saying she felt alone in a full hostel. I've left a note under her door with the counselling centre's evening hours, and I'll check in at breakfast.
Elizabeth

qa.q: How long did Disha's boyfriend wait at the gate?
qa.a: For an hour.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as she held a book without turning a page?
qa.a: She seemed tense and lonely, avoiding a deep talk while feeling alone in a full hostel.

qa.q: How is Elizabeth supporting Disha?
qa.a: By leaving the counselling centre's hours under her door and planning a breakfast check-in, without pushing.

qa.q: What is it like for the boyfriend to wait an hour and get "busy"?
qa.a: He probably feels hurt and shut out, wanting to talk about the relationship and getting no answer.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who guards independence and avoids a deep conversation, while lonely inside.

passage:
Tuesday, 11.40 p.m. Parul asked tonight if we could spend Diwali with her family in Lucknow. I said I had a project, which is half true. Then she said, softly, "Sometimes it feels like you keep one foot out the door." I laughed it off and went home early. Now I'm lying here with the fan clicking, and I feel horrible, and also relieved, which is worse. I tell everyone I love my freedom. I do. But tonight the flat is so quiet I can hear the fridge. What scares me isn't Parul. It's how much I'd miss her if I let myself lean. Maybe I'll text her in the morning: "Sorry I left. Can we talk?"
Elizabeth

qa.q: Where does Parul's family live?
qa.a: In Lucknow.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Elizabeth describe after leaving early?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels horrible and relieved at once, and scared of how much it would hurt to depend on Parul.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth try next?
qa.a: Send the planned message and share a little of the fear with Parul, instead of leaving again.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when Elizabeth laughs off her words?
qa.a: Parul probably feels hurt and brushed aside, having said something honest and vulnerable.

grounding: Shows a young adult who avoids deep talk and leaves when a partner asks for more, while fearing dependence and feeling lonely.

passage:
Hansa: can we talk tonight? about us, like where this is going
Jahnavi: haha heavy. there's a gig on friday, want to come?
Hansa: I'd like that. but I'd also like an answer
Jahnavi: I don't really do the whole "what are we" thing
Hansa: ok. I'm not asking you to give up your freedom
Jahnavi: I think I need some space this week
Hansa: that's the third time you've said that when I ask something real
(no reply for an hour)
Jahnavi: sorry. honestly when people need more from me I panic and want to run
Jahnavi: and then I sit alone in my room and feel lonely anyway
Hansa: thank you for saying that. we can go slow. Friday gig, and we talk after?
Jahnavi: ok. slow is good

qa.q: What does Jahnavi invite Hansa to on Friday?
qa.a: A gig.

qa.q: What is Jahnavi feeling behind the need for space?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels panicky when someone needs more and afraid of depending on them, and then lonely when alone.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that made it easier for Jahnavi to open up?
qa.a: Hansa stated the pattern calmly, thanked Jahnavi for being honest, and offered to go slow with a clear next step.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel hearing "I need some space" a third time?
qa.a: Hansa may feel hurt and shut out, especially since it comes whenever something real is asked.

grounding: Shows a young adult who avoids deep talk and seeks space when asked for more, while feeling panic and loneliness inside.
